title: S3-like Object Storage
oneLine: Keep namespace metadata strongly controlled, stream object bytes directly to placement-selected data nodes, verify checksums, and use replication or erasure coding with background repair.
opening: I would split the control plane from the byte path. The API layer authenticates and authorizes bucket/object operations, while a strongly consistent metadata service owns namespace, versions, multipart sessions, object manifests, and placement references. Uploads stream chunks directly to data nodes or a blob layer selected by a placement service that understands capacity and failure domains. Each chunk is checksummed, replicated synchronously for small/hot objects or encoded with erasure coding for large/cold data, then the metadata commit atomically publishes the object version. Reads resolve metadata, choose healthy replicas/fragments, verify integrity, and support range requests. Heartbeats and scrubbers detect loss/corruption, repair runs in the background, deletes create tombstones and later garbage collection, and LIST is served from partitioned ordered metadata rather than scanning data nodes.
ask: Object sizes, total objects, throughput, and durability target?
PUT/GET/DELETE/LIST, versioning, range reads, multipart, lifecycle?
Single region or cross-region replication and compliance?
scale: Metadata cardinality is object count; byte storage is object size—small-object systems can be metadata-bound.
Durability comes from independent failure domains plus continuous detection/repair, not replication factor alone.
Erasure coding lowers storage overhead but increases CPU/network and small-read complexity.

decisions.why: Namespace uniqueness, version publication, multipart completion, and LIST semantics need one authoritative outcome.
decisions.switch: Derived inventory/catalog can be eventually consistent, but not object identity itself.

decisions.default: Replication for small/hot/latency-sensitive objects; erasure coding for large/cold objects.
decisions.why: Replication gives simple fast reads; erasure coding saves capacity at repair/CPU/network cost.
decisions.switch: Policy can transition objects asynchronously through lifecycle tiers.

decisions.default: Capacity- and topology-aware deterministic placement with a versioned map.
decisions.why: Replicas/fragments must span disks, hosts, racks/AZs and avoid hotspots.
decisions.switch: Consistent hashing is a useful primitive but needs weighting and failure-domain rules.

decisions.default: Data first, then atomic metadata commit makes the version visible.
decisions.why: Readers never observe a manifest pointing to incomplete bytes.
decisions.switch: Uncommitted uploads are hidden and garbage-collected after a grace period.

deepDives.title: Multipart upload
points: Create session, upload numbered parts independently with checksums, list/retry parts, then complete with an ordered manifest.
Completion is idempotent and atomically creates a version.
Abort/expired sessions leave reclaimable unreferenced parts.

deepDives.title: Integrity and repair
points: Checksum at client/transport/chunk and scrub periodically at rest.
Read from another replica on mismatch and enqueue repair.
Track repair backlog and durability risk by failure domain.

deepDives.title: Small objects
points: Millions of tiny files cause metadata and random-I/O overhead.
Pack small objects into larger segments with an index or dedicate a small-object tier.
Garbage collection then compacts segments rather than deleting one file at a time.

deepDives.title: LIST and deletion
points: Partition ordered metadata by bucket/prefix and paginate with opaque continuation tokens.
Delete writes a versioned tombstone; legal hold/version retention may keep data.
Physical reclamation is asynchronous and safe only after no metadata/version references remain.

failures.response: Write to alternate placement, require durability quorum before publish, and repair under-replicated chunks.

failures.risk: Metadata committed but data corrupts later
failures.response: Checksums, replicated/erasure fragments, background scrub, read repair, and durability-risk alerts.
Version/epoch on routes, data-node redirect or rejection, refresh control-plane map, and idempotent retry.
Versioned metadata state, leases/preconditions, tombstone semantics, and delayed physical GC.

questions.q: Why not store objects in a distributed filesystem?
questions.a: Object storage exposes immutable key-based blobs, decouples metadata from placement, scales namespace independently, and avoids POSIX locking/rename semantics. A distributed filesystem may implement the lower layer but has a different API contract.

questions.q: How do you achieve eleven nines durability?
questions.a: Independent failure-domain placement, checksums, continuous scrubbing, rapid repair, conservative deletion, tested restore, and operational risk controls. It is an end-to-end probability target, not simply ‘three copies.’

questions.q: How do range reads work with erasure coding?
questions.a: Map byte range to stripes/fragments, fetch enough fragments—prefer data fragments without reconstruction—and verify. Small ranges may suffer amplification, which is why hot/small objects often use replication.
The metadata commit is strongly consistent and only references durable data. Subsequent reads resolve the committed version; caches use versioned keys/ETags to avoid stale overwrite results.

mistakes: Treating data nodes as the namespace source of truth
Publishing metadata before bytes are durable
Saying three replicas automatically imply extreme durability
seniorSignal: Explain the publication invariant, placement topology, integrity evidence, repair loop, metadata/list scaling, and lifecycle economics. Durability is a continuous process.
implementation: Consensus-backed metadata shards (Raft) and versioned placement service
Chunk servers/object nodes with checksums, replication and erasure coding
Multipart signed upload, ETags, preconditions, range GET
Scrubber/repair/lifecycle workers with object-store-style inventory and audit
